Let’s dive into Chapter 10—Sustaining Brevity: Reflection, Feedback, and Growth.
You know, like any skill, keeping your communication brief takes ongoing effort and a little bit of self-awareness. It’s so easy to slip back into old habits, especially when you’re under pressure or handling something complex. That’s where regular reflection and feedback come in—they help you keep your practice sharp and evolving.
One way to do this is by setting aside time—maybe every few weeks—to review how you’re communicating, either on your own or with your team. Are your messages starting to get a little wordy? Are meetings wandering off track? Noticing these patterns gives you a chance to reset, adjust expectations, and try out new strategies together.
Here are a few simple tools you can use to keep brevity alive:
First, create feedback loops. Ask your colleagues for honest thoughts about whether your messages are clear and to the point.
Next, try a self-audit. Take a look at a week’s worth of your emails or meeting notes. Are there places where you could’ve said more with less?
You can also turn team discussions into learning moments. Share examples where someone nailed it with a short, effective message—or where things got a little muddled and wordy.
And don’t forget to celebrate progress, even the small wins. A little recognition goes a long way in building good habits.
It’s also really helpful to keep an open mind. The way we communicate is always changing, thanks to new technology and shifting workplace norms. So why not experiment? Try out new formats or tools, and share what you discover with others.
Above all, remember—brevity isn’t a finish line you cross, it’s a journey you’re always on. Every email or conversation is a new chance to practice, learn, and get better.
When you stay intentional and mindful, you’re not just making your point—you’re making a real impact.
